GORD = Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.  It is a condition where the acidic contents of the stomach leak out into the oesophagus (gullet). This can cause heartburn or indigestion.  Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which works by stopping the production of acid within the stomach. It does this by blocking the H+K+ATPase system, known as the acid pump, which is responsible for producing acid in the stomach.  Gaviscon contains alginates which are insoluble in gastric juices and form a physical barrier on top of the acidic contents of the stomach. This prevents the reflux of acid into the oesophagus.  Gaviscon is useful for treating occasional heartburn but not chronic cases.  NICE guidelines state that PPIs should be offered before antacids like Gaviscon for the treatment of GORD.  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg184/chapter/1-Gastro-oesophageal-reflux-disease-GORD-and-barrett%E2%80%99s-oesophagus-assessment-and-diagnosis#treatment-options-for-gastro-oesophageal-reflux-disease-gord-or-heartburn-that-does-not-require-urgent-inv

C3a and C5a are the two main chemotaxins. They are both anaphylatoxins as well as inflammatory mediators. They also cause degranulation of mast cells and basophils. C3b is involved in opsonisation. It binds to pathogens and triggers immune responses. It is then bound by antibodies which trigger its activation into C3c. C3c then goes on to form C3bBb which is the final complex needed for opsonisation. This happens in the blood or lymphatic vessels. C3f is also produced during opsonisation but it is not clear what function it has. C3d is involved in the adaptive response. It binds to antigen-presenting cells (such as dendritic cells) and acts as a T cell ligand. It also binds to B cells and activates them. C4 is activated when C3b has bound to a pathogen. It cleaves the pathogen into smaller peptides which act as antigens. These antigens then bind to MHC class I on the dendritic cell. They all attack the carbonyl group on the amide linkage of the peptide bonds. Carboxypeptidase attacks the C-terminal end peptides. This is because this end has a free amine group that is negatively charged and therefore attracted to the positively charged enzyme.The other enzymes attack the amide linkage of the peptide bond. This is because it is the side chain of the amino acid in the peptide bond that interacts with the enzyme not the carbonyl group. Peptide bonds have a partial double bond character. Therefore, they are planar structures with no free electrons around the carbonyl carbon. The electronegative oxygen of the carbonyl group is able to make a H-bond with the hydrogen attached to the nitrogen in the amide linkage. This interaction is what weakens the bond between the two amino acids. The side chains of the amino acids help to further stabilise the peptide bond through interactions with each other. These interactions are what give each type of protein its unique ability. For example, proteins involved in DNA replication contain a lot of histones (positively charged) and arginines (negatively charged). The ptosis following loss of sympathetic innervation to the superior tarsal muscle will be partial as the orbicularis oculi and inferior tarsal muscle are still supplied by parasympathetic innervation. This is known as Bell's phenomenon. Bell's Phenomenon is the result of damage to the nerves supplying the superior tarsal muscle. The eye will open normally but cannot close completely. The lower eyelid may appear to roll outwards when the eye is closed. The reason that this occurs is because there is only parasympathetic innervation to the orbicularis oculi and inferior tarsal muscles. This loss of innervation to the levator palpebrae superioris muscle usually results from damage to cranial nerve III or IV. It can also occur secondary to other conditions such as Grave’s disease. A pulmonary shunt occurs when a portion of the blood supply bypasses the alveoli without coming into contact with the gas within them. This means that the oxygenation of the blood does not occur in these areas and so low pi02 values are expected.  B- VQ mismatch is caused by ventilation perfusion inequality where the blood flow to the alveoli does not match the airflow in the alveoli. This causes a high pi02 and a low piCO2 as the CO2 remains in the blood for longer and the O2 dissociates from the haemoglobin quicker. C- The correct answer as it shows a pulmonary shunt has occurred due to the increased ventilation (high piCO2) and decreased oxygenation (low piO2). D- Diffusion impairment occurs when there is a problem with the diffusion of gases across the membrane of the alveolus and this presents itself with low piO2 and high piCO2. E- Hypoventilation is when the volume of ventilated air is too small or the rate of ventilation is too slow. This causes a high piCO2 and a low piO2.  *The reason why I didn't include type 2 respiratory failure is because the symptoms of this are high piCO2 and low piO2. Type 1 respiratory failure only presents with low piO2. Also if the piCO2 had been low then it would suggest a problem with the ventilation part of the equation rather than the oxygenation part so the cause would be more likely to be a pulmonary shunt or diffusion impairment.  *Also if the piO2 had been high then this would indicate a problem with oxygenation which rules out all problems with the ventilation side of things including VQ mismatch. This would leave the cause being either a pulmonary shunt or diffusion impairment.  *I chose to make the piCO2 normal as if it were high then the condition could be either hypoventilation or VQ mismatch.
